title: Figma foundations: tidy files, flexible layouts, calm visuals

say: Figma foundations: tidy files, flexible layouts and calm visuals.
This is the video for module one of UI Design with Figma.
A UX flow tells you what a product must do. A wireframe shows the rough layout in grey boxes.

A wireframe shows rough grey boxes

say: UI design turns that into the exact interface a developer will build: real colours, real fonts, exact spacing in pixels, and every button state.
Figma runs in a web browser, so a client, a developer and you can open the same file at the same time.

panel.heading: From a UX flow to buildable screens
items: A UX flow says what the product does
A wireframe shows rough grey boxes

say: A finished handover has screens for every step, including empty, loading and error states.
It has foundations, the colour, type and spacing values, and components like buttons and cards, built once and reused.
And it has a prototype a client can tap through, plus specs and assets a developer can use without calling you.

Clients judge your professionalism the moment they open the file. For example, Amaka sets up a practice app called Oja Fresh with six pages: Cover, Foundations, Components, Screens, Prototype and Archive.

say: A beginner's screen looks fine at one size and breaks at every other. With a manual frame, you move each item by hand, and longer text overlaps.

panel.heading: Manual frame or auto layout?
left: You move each item by hand
right: Items stack by gap and padding

say: Auto layout, Shift plus A, turns a frame into a flexible stack. You choose a direction, a gap between items, and padding inside. New items slot in, and spacing stays the same everywhere.

panel.heading: Manual frame or auto layout?
left: You move each item by hand
right: Items stack by gap and padding

say: Each element gets a resizing rule. Hug contents means the frame fits what is inside, so a button grows with its label.

cards.d: The frame fits what is inside. A button grows when Add becomes Add to cart.
The child stretches to the space its parent gives it, like a card's text column.
An exact size that does not change, such as a 64 × 64 product photo.

say: Fill container means it stretches to take the space its parent gives it.

panel.rule: Always test at 360 px wide as well as your main device.

say: Polished screens repeat a few decisions. Use an 8-point system: spacing in multiples of 8, with 4 for small gaps. Only these values are allowed.

panel.heading: Spacing and a type scale
items: Save each size as a text style

say: For text, start with a body size of 16 and multiply by 1.25 for each step up.

panel.heading: Spacing and a type scale
items: Save each size as a text style

say: 16 becomes 20, then 25, then 31.25. Amaka rounds them to 20, 24 and 32, and saves each as a text style. If the client wants bigger text, she edits Body once and every screen updates.

panel.heading: Spacing and a type scale
items: Save each size as a text style

say: Name colours by role, like primary, surface and error, so a rebrand changes values, not meaning.
Keep tap targets at least 48 by 48. Use strong contrast, because people check orders in bright sunlight. Remember every large photo costs data.
And type real local words with tone marks before choosing a font. Empty boxes mean the font does not support them.

panel.heading: Design for your real users
items: Name colours by role, like Primary, Error
Type real Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa words

say: To remember. Organise with pages, sections and plain names. Use auto layout for anything that stacks, with Hug, Fill and Fixed.
Define spacing, type and colour roles once. And test at 360 px with real local text.
